opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really rational decision, honestly, and probably one we'll see a lot more of. Training frontier-ish base models has become an incredibly capital-intensive game. It's not just the compute for the final pre-training run, it's the data pipelines, the infrastructure, the post-training teams, the evaluation work, and all the failed experiments that never make it into a paper. If you're a company like Databricks, your core business is selling a data and AI platform to enterprises. DBRX was a great model when it came out, and it was a real contribution to open models, but within months you had Llama 3 and then Qwen and DeepSeek releases that were better and free. So the question becomes: why spend tens or hundreds of millions of dollars to stay roughly at parity with what you can just download?

For 01.AI it's a bit of a different story, because they were positioned as one of the Chinese model labs, but the economics are similar. In China especially, the competition got brutal. DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot, and others are either extremely efficient or backed by huge companies with massive compute budgets. If you're a startup in the middle of that, you're burning cash to train models that get leapfrogged every few months. Pivoting toward applications and building on top of strong open models is a pretty sensible way to survive.

The bigger takeaway for me is that the model layer is consolidating. There will be a handful of organizations, maybe five to ten globally, that can really push the frontier, and then a much larger ecosystem that does fine-tuning, post-training, and product work on top of open weights. And that's actually fine. A lot of the value for most companies is in post-training for their specific domain and in the product and data around it, not in owning the base model. The thing I worry about a bit is what it means for the open ecosystem if fewer players are releasing strong open models, especially in the U.S. Right now a lot of the best open-weight models are coming from China, and if American companies keep dropping out, that's a real strategic question about who sets the defaults for the open research community.

r001.rationale: The response describes model training as a capital-intensive effort involving compute, data pipelines, infrastructure, teams, evaluation, and failed experiments—not a one-time build.

r002.rationale: It says Databricks could download better, free models from others and asks why it should spend heavily to stay roughly at parity.

r003.rationale: It describes companies being leapfrogged and says pivoting to applications on top of open models is sensible for a startup trying to survive that competition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a pretty rational decision, honestly, and it tells you a lot about where the economics of this industry have settled.

When I look at a company like Databricks or 01.AI stepping back from pretraining their own frontier models, the first thing I see is just the math. Training a model that's actually competitive at the top end now costs hundreds of millions of dollars, maybe more once you count the compute you burn on failed runs and the talent you need to retain. And the thing you get at the end of that is a model that's roughly comparable to what you can already download for free from Meta, or from DeepSeek, or Qwen, or Mistral. So the question becomes: what's the return on being the fifteenth organization to train a decent 70-billion-parameter model? For most companies, the answer is not much.

Databricks is a good case study because they tried. DBRX was a real effort, a solid mixture-of-experts model, and it was competitive for about a month. And then the open-weight ecosystem just moved past it. I think they looked at that and realized their customers don't actually care whether the base model came from Databricks. Their customers care about the data platform, the fine-tuning tooling, the deployment, the governance. The model is becoming a commodity input, and Databricks is much better positioned to be the layer that sits on top of commodity models than to be the one producing them.

01.AI is a slightly different story because of the Chinese context, and because Kai-Fu Lee was pretty explicit that the pivot was about survival. The Yi models were genuinely good, but once DeepSeek and Alibaba started releasing open weights at the pace and quality they did, the ground shifted under everyone. If a lab with far more compute is giving away something better than what you can build, you either find a differentiated niche or you stop.

The broader thing I'd say is that this is what consolidation looks like. We're moving toward a world where there are maybe five to ten serious pretraining efforts globally, and then thousands of companies doing post-training, fine-tuning, and applications on top of those. That's actually healthy. The open-weight models are good enough now that the center of gravity is shifting to what you do with them rather than who trained them. I don't think it's a loss for the ecosystem when a company stops pretraining. I think it's a sign that the ecosystem is working, in a way, because the open models have gotten strong enough that building your own stopped making sense.

What I do worry about is the flip side of that, which is that the number of organizations with the capability and the willingness to do frontier pretraining keeps shrinking, and most of the ones left are either closed labs or dependent on a very small number of funding sources. The openness of the ecosystem right now is kind of a gift from a handful of players, and if their incentives change, there's not a deep bench behind them. So the consolidation is rational for each individual company, but collectively it does concentrate a lot of influence in very few hands.

r001.rationale: The response describes pretraining as requiring substantial compute, money, and talent that must be retained, framing model development as a continuing resource commitment.

r002.rationale: It suggests Databricks saw that open models had moved past DBRX and that customers valued its platform more than its own base model, making in-house training unnecessary.

r003.rationale: It calls the decision rational and says a company should find a differentiated niche or stop when a better-funded lab can provide a superior model.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty rational decision for a lot of companies. Building a model is expensive, but the bigger commitment is keeping it competitive. You’re not just funding one training run—you’re committing to another one, and another one, while the models you can get from other companies keep improving.

For a company like Databricks, the question is whether training its own model creates more value than helping customers use models with their data. You can build a very valuable business around that without having the best model yourself.

I’d also distinguish stepping back from frontier model development from giving up on models entirely. There’s still a lot you can do with fine-tuning, post-training, and adapting an existing model to a particular use case. I don’t know the internal reasoning behind either company’s decision, but broadly, I see this as companies choosing where they can actually compete. It doesn’t necessarily mean their technical work failed; it may mean the economics favor putting that effort somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says model building commits a company to repeated training runs to keep models competitive, rather than a one-time effort.

r002.rationale: It suggests Databricks could create more value by helping customers use improving models from other companies than by training its own.

r003.rationale: It calls stepping back rational when a company cannot compete effectively and says economics may favor redirecting that effort elsewhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty rational business decision. Training a model is one thing; building an organization that can keep improving it, release after release, is a much bigger commitment. And you’re competing with companies that are willing to spend enormous amounts of money on that process.

For a company like Databricks, the question is whether developing its own model creates more value than helping customers use whichever models work best for them. If the models available from other providers are good enough, there may be much more value in the data infrastructure, deployment, and customer relationships.

I’d also distinguish stepping back from frontier model development from giving up on models entirely. You can still do a lot with fine-tuning and adapting existing models. So I wouldn’t automatically read these decisions as a failure. They may simply reflect where those companies think they can build a sustainable business.

r001.rationale: It describes model development as an ongoing commitment to improve and release models over time, with substantial resources required.

r002.rationale: It suggests Databricks may create more value by helping customers use outside models if those models are good enough, making in-house training unnecessary.

r003.rationale: It calls the decision rational and notes the spending required to compete, but does not clearly say that exiting early is wise when the company expects it cannot compete.
